prompt: Why did Alexander Hamilton urge Congress in 1791 to enact protective tariffs on European goods?

options.text: To shield young American factories from British price competition
To force southern planters to abandon cotton and tobacco exports
To replace the U.S. dollar with French silver coinage nationwide
To ban all maritime trade between New England and Caribbean ports

explanation: In his Report on Manufactures, Hamilton argued that tariffs would nurture infant U.S. industries until they could compete globally.

trap_notes.b: Hamilton wanted to balance agriculture with industry, not end farm exports.
trap_notes.c: Hamilton established the U.S. Mint and a domestic dollar, not French coinage.
trap_notes.d: Tariffs taxed imports rather than banning regional maritime commerce.
trap_notes.default: Hamilton used protective tariffs to help infant American manufacturers grow.

prompt: How did opening the Erie Canal in 1825 reshape the economy of the early United States?

options.text: It shifted most U.S. cotton exports away from New Orleans
It slashed freight costs between the Great Lakes and New York
It ended steamboat traffic along the lower Mississippi River
It blocked European immigrants from settling the Midwest

explanation: The Erie Canal cut shipping costs from Buffalo to New York City by roughly 90 percent, linking Midwest farms to Atlantic trade.

trap_notes.a: Southern cotton still moved through Gulf ports like New Orleans and Mobile.
trap_notes.c: Mississippi steamboat commerce continued growing alongside northern canals.
trap_notes.d: The canal actually accelerated westward migration into the Great Lakes basin.
trap_notes.default: Lower canal freight rates integrated Midwest grain with New York's port.

prompt: How did the Homestead Act and Pacific Railway Act of 1862 work together to expand U.S. output?

options.text: They nationalized all eastern factories to fund western forts
They taxed frontier farms to subsidize coastal clipper ships
They paired free land grants with rail lines to distant markets
They outlawed private land ownership west of the Mississippi

explanation: Free 160-acre homesteads drew settlers west while transcontinental railroads carried their grain and cattle to eastern cities.

trap_notes.a: Neither law nationalized eastern manufacturing plants.
trap_notes.b: The laws subsidized overland railroads, not coastal sailing ships.
trap_notes.d: The Homestead Act transferred federal public land into private family ownership.
trap_notes.default: Land grants brought settlers while railroads connected western farms to markets.

prompt: What market failure did Congress target when it passed the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890?

options.text: Seasonal crop failures caused by Great Plains droughts
Gold shortages inside local frontier general stores
High municipal property taxes on small family farms
Monopolistic trusts restricting output and fixing prices

explanation: The Sherman Antitrust Act outlawed contracts and conspiracies in restraint of trade to curb Gilded Age monopolies.

trap_notes.a: Weather-driven crop losses are supply shocks, not antitrust violations.
trap_notes.b: Currency supply debates involved silver and gold standards, not antitrust law.
trap_notes.c: Local property taxes fall under state and city law, not federal antitrust.
trap_notes.default: Antitrust law targets monopolies that stifle competition and fix prices.

prompt: Why did Congress create the Federal Reserve System in 1913 after the financial Panic of 1907?

options.text: To provide an elastic currency and lender of last resort
To insure every stock portfolio against market losses
To eliminate all state-chartered commercial banks
To replace federal income taxes with bank reserve fees

explanation: The 1913 Federal Reserve Act created a central bank able to supply emergency liquidity during banking panics.

trap_notes.b: The Fed stabilizes banking liquidity; it does not insure stock investors.
trap_notes.c: State-chartered banks continued operating within the dual banking system.
trap_notes.d: The 16th Amendment in 1913 authorized the federal income tax separately.
trap_notes.default: Congress created the Fed to stabilize banking panics as lender of last resort.

prompt: How did the U.S. Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 deepen the global Great Depression?

options.text: It eliminated all customs duties on European steel
It sparked foreign retaliatory tariffs that shrank world trade
It forced the Federal Reserve to print unlimited paper dollars
It doubled American farm exports to Western Europe

explanation: Raising U.S. tariffs to historic highs prompted trading partners to retaliate, collapsing global imports and exports.

trap_notes.a: Smoot-Hawley sharply raised tariffs rather than cutting them.
trap_notes.c: Tariff policy was fiscal trade law, not central bank money printing.
trap_notes.d: Retaliatory tariffs crushed U.S. agricultural exports instead of doubling them.
trap_notes.default: Retaliatory tariffs turned protectionism into a global trade collapse.

prompt: How did creating the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) in 1933 stop contagious bank runs?

options.text: It banned households from opening checking accounts
It required banks to hold 100 percent gold reserves
It guaranteed insured deposits even if a bank failed
It merged every private bank into the U.S. Treasury

explanation: Deposit insurance reassured savers that their money was safe, removing the panic incentive to withdraw cash all at once.

trap_notes.a: The FDIC encouraged trust in checking and savings accounts.
trap_notes.b: Banks still operated on fractional reserves rather than 100 percent gold.
trap_notes.d: Private commercial banks remained privately owned and regulated.
trap_notes.default: Federal deposit insurance ended panic withdrawals by protecting savers.

prompt: How did the 1944 GI Bill boost long-run U.S. productivity after World War II?

options.text: It raised import tariffs on foreign consumer electronics
It restricted veterans to working only in defense plants
It froze consumer wages across all manufacturing sectors
It funded college tuition and home loans for veterans

explanation: By financing education and mortgages, the GI Bill expanded human capital and stimulated postwar construction.

trap_notes.a: The GI Bill focused on veteran benefits, not trade tariffs.
trap_notes.b: Veterans used benefits to enter diverse civilian professions and trades.
trap_notes.c: Wartime wage controls ended after WWII rather than being extended by the GI Bill.
trap_notes.default: College and housing subsidies under the GI Bill built postwar human capital.

prompt: What major economic effect followed the 1956 Federal-Aid Highway Act building the Interstate System?

options.text: Lower trucking costs and faster suburban commercial growth
A complete halt to domestic airline passenger travel
A sharp decline in automobile and oil consumption
The immediate closure of all coastal container ports

explanation: Limited-access interstates cut overland freight times, expanded national supply chains, and fueled suburban development.

trap_notes.b: Commercial jet travel expanded alongside interstate highway trucking.
trap_notes.c: Interstate highways increased demand for cars, trucks, and motor fuel.
trap_notes.d: Highways fed cargo to and from seaports rather than closing them.
trap_notes.default: Interstate highways lowered freight costs and reshaped metro growth.

prompt: Why did the 1973 Arab oil embargo trigger stagflation across the United States?

options.text: Cheap gasoline caused factories to hire too many workers
Soaring energy costs pushed prices up while slowing output
Higher U.S. oil exports caused severe currency deflation
Congress eliminated all federal income taxes overnight

explanation: The oil supply shock raised production and transport costs across the economy, causing both inflation and recession.

trap_notes.a: Oil prices quadrupled rather than falling, squeezing business margins.
trap_notes.c: The U.S. was a net oil importer facing inflation, not deflation.
trap_notes.d: Congress did not abolish income taxes during the 1973 oil crisis.
trap_notes.default: An adverse energy supply shock drives inflation up and output down.

prompt: What global monetary shift occurred when President Nixon ended dollar-to-gold convertibility in 1971?

options.text: Every country returned to using silver coins for trade
The International Monetary Fund banned foreign exchange
Major currencies moved toward floating exchange rates
Gold mines in South Africa closed permanently

explanation: Ending the Bretton Woods gold link ushered in today's fiat system where major currencies float on market supply and demand.

trap_notes.a: Countries moved away from metallic backing toward fiat currencies.
trap_notes.b: Foreign exchange trading expanded rapidly once exchange rates floated.
trap_notes.d: Gold remained a traded commodity and reserve asset even without fixed pegs.
trap_notes.default: Ending dollar-gold convertibility ended Bretton Woods fixed exchange rates.

prompt: Why did Congress and the Treasury launch the 2008 TARP program during the subprime mortgage crisis?

options.text: To raise mortgage rates and slow down home construction
To replace private homeownership with federal housing
To outlaw all adjustable-rate loans across the country
To inject capital into banks and prevent credit freeze

explanation: TARP purchased troubled assets and bank equity to keep major financial institutions solvent and prevent a wider credit collapse.

trap_notes.a: Policymakers cut interest rates in 2008 to support borrowing, not raise rates.
trap_notes.b: TARP stabilized private banks rather than nationalizing housing.
trap_notes.c: Later Dodd-Frank rules tightened standards without banning all ARMs.
trap_notes.default: TARP recapitalized banks to stop a systemic financial freeze.

prompt: How did massive silver mining at Potosi and Zacatecas reshape early modern global trade?

options.text: Spanish silver flowed to Europe and Asia to buy Asian goods
European prices fell sharply due to scarce coinage
Ming China banned silver taxes and returned to barter
Silk Road caravans replaced all Atlantic sailing ships

explanation: American silver financed European imports of Chinese silk, tea, and porcelain while fueling price inflation in Europe.

trap_notes.b: Abundant silver caused the 16th-century Price Revolution (inflation), not deflation.
trap_notes.c: Ming China's Single Whip tax reform actually increased demand for silver.
trap_notes.d: Transoceanic galleons expanded maritime trade over overland caravans.
trap_notes.default: New World silver lubricated early modern trade between Europe, the Americas, and Asia.

prompt: What financial innovation did the Dutch East India Company (VOC) pioneer in 1602 to fund risky voyages?

options.text: Tax-free municipal bonds backed by farmland
Tradable joint-stock shares with limited liability
Paper banknotes redeemable only in spices
State-owned steamships insured by the League of Nations

explanation: The VOC issued permanent shares traded on the Amsterdam exchange, letting many investors pool capital and share risk.

trap_notes.a: The VOC raised private merchant equity rather than local farmland bonds.
trap_notes.c: VOC shares represented equity ownership, not spice-backed currency.
trap_notes.d: Steamships and the League of Nations belonged to the 19th and 20th centuries.
trap_notes.default: Joint-stock shares allowed investors to pool capital and trade ownership.

prompt: How did Britain's Enclosure Acts contribute to the Industrial Revolution?

options.text: They gave every peasant free factory machinery
They banned steam engines inside northern cities
They displaced small farmers into urban factory labor
They eliminated private property rights in rural counties

explanation: Fencing common lands raised farm efficiency while pushing landless rural workers to seek wage jobs in industrial towns.

trap_notes.a: Enclosure consolidated land for wealthy landlords rather than gifting machines.
trap_notes.b: Steam-powered textile mills expanded rapidly during enclosure.
trap_notes.d: Enclosure strengthened private land titles by ending shared commons.
trap_notes.default: Enclosure freed up labor that migrated to growing industrial cities.

prompt: Why did British manufacturers push Parliament to repeal the Corn Laws in 1846?

options.text: To raise tariffs on American cotton and wool
To stop urban workers from migrating to London
To force colonies to buy expensive British grain
To lower food prices and support free-trade exports

explanation: Repealing grain tariffs lowered bread costs for factory workers and encouraged foreign countries to buy British manufactured goods.

trap_notes.a: Manufacturers wanted cheaper imported raw materials and food, not higher tariffs.
trap_notes.b: Factory owners welcomed urban labor rather than blocking migration.
trap_notes.c: Britain imported grain; it was not trying to export high-priced grain.
trap_notes.default: Repealing the Corn Laws lowered food costs and advanced British free trade.

prompt: What monetary policy caused Weimar Germany's catastrophic hyperinflation in 1923?

options.text: Printing massive sums of paper marks to pay deficits
Raising interest rates to 50 percent to curb spending
Fixing the mark strictly to British gold sovereigns
Collecting huge budget surpluses from German factories

explanation: To fund Ruhr strike subsidies and fiscal deficits, the Reichsbank printed currency rapidly, destroying the mark's purchasing power.

trap_notes.b: Sharp interest rate hikes cool inflation rather than causing hyperinflation.
trap_notes.c: The mark was unbacked paper currency in 1923 until the Rentenmark stabilized it.
trap_notes.d: Large budget deficits, not surpluses, drove the money-printing spiral.
trap_notes.default: Rapidly printing unbacked money to cover deficits fuels hyperinflation.

prompt: How did the U.S. Marshall Plan of 1948 aid both Western Europe and the American economy?

options.text: It required Europe to dismantle all industrial factories
It rebuilt European infrastructure and created U.S. export buyers
It replaced European currencies with the Soviet ruble
It raised steep tariffs between France and West Germany

explanation: Grants and loans financed European recovery, restoring stable trading partners for American machinery, grain, and goods.

trap_notes.a: The Marshall Plan rebuilt European industry rather than dismantling it.
trap_notes.c: The plan anchored Western Europe to dollar-linked trade, not the Soviet ruble.
trap_notes.d: The program encouraged European economic integration and lower trade barriers.
trap_notes.default: Rebuilding Europe created prosperous, stable trading partners for the U.S.

prompt: How did Deng Xiaoping's 1978 reforms transform China's coastal cities into export powerhouses?

options.text: By banning foreign direct investment in coastal ports
By eliminating all private household farming plots
By opening Special Economic Zones to foreign capital and trade
By closing Shanghai's port to international container ships

explanation: Special Economic Zones offered tax incentives and market rules that attracted foreign factories, technology, and export jobs.

trap_notes.a: Reforms actively welcomed foreign direct investment for the first time since 1949.
trap_notes.b: Deng replaced collective farms with the household responsibility system.
trap_notes.d: Coastal ports expanded rapidly as China embraced export-led growth.
trap_notes.default: Special Economic Zones combined market incentives with global export access.

prompt: What economic tradeoff did European nations accept when adopting the euro under the Maastricht Treaty?

options.text: Higher tariffs on goods shipped between France and Germany
Loss of free labor movement across member borders
Complete abolition of all national income and sales taxes
Giving up independent national monetary policy for one currency

explanation: Eurozone members gained lower currency-exchange costs but ceded interest-rate control to the European Central Bank.

trap_notes.a: The European single market eliminated internal tariffs rather than raising them.
trap_notes.b: EU integration expanded cross-border labor mobility rather than ending it.
trap_notes.c: Member nations retained their own national tax and fiscal budgets.
trap_notes.default: Sharing one currency removes exchange costs but ends national rate control.

prompt: What triggered the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis starting in Thailand?

options.text: Collapse of a fixed currency peg amid heavy foreign-dollar debt
A sudden ban on semiconductor exports from South Korea
Discovery of massive gold reserves inside the Mekong Delta
Hyperinflation caused by zero foreign borrowing

explanation: When Thailand ran out of reserves to defend its dollar peg, the baht plunged and made dollar-denominated loans unaffordable.

trap_notes.b: Asian electronics exports stayed strong and later helped economies recover.
trap_notes.c: The crisis stemmed from currency and debt mismatches, not gold discoveries.
trap_notes.d: Heavy short-term foreign borrowing, not zero borrowing, created fragility.
trap_notes.default: Devaluing a pegged currency spikes the local cost of foreign-currency debt.

prompt: How did China's 2001 entry into the World Trade Organization affect global manufacturing?

options.text: It raised average tariffs on Chinese goods in North America
It integrated China's vast labor force into global supply chains
It ended container shipping across the Pacific Ocean
It forced European factories to stop exporting machinery

explanation: WTO membership locked in lower tariffs and predictable trade rules, accelerating global offshoring and consumer price declines.

trap_notes.a: WTO accession lowered trade barriers rather than raising tariffs.
trap_notes.c: Trans-Pacific container shipping surged after 2001.
trap_notes.d: European machinery exports to China's growing factories actually expanded.
trap_notes.default: WTO rules integrated China into global production and lowered goods prices.

prompt: Why did Silk Road merchants rely on high-value, low-weight goods like silk and spices?

options.text: Roman law prohibited transporting any metal coins overland
Camels could only travel during winter snowstorms
High overland transport costs made bulky goods unprofitable
Central Asian oasis cities produced no local food

explanation: Long caravan journeys across deserts and mountains made shipping grain or timber too costly, favoring luxury goods.

trap_notes.a: Roman gold and silver coins traveled widely along Eurasian trade routes.
trap_notes.b: Caravans crossed deserts in milder seasons and relied on oasis relays.
trap_notes.d: Oasis towns supplied food and water to passing merchant caravans.
trap_notes.default: High overland freight costs restricted caravan trade to high-value goods.

prompt: What monetary lesson illustrates Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage spending in Cairo?

options.text: Gold coins lose value only when governments ban trade
Taxing caravan routes eliminates local inflation
Shortages of precious metals cause rapid price inflation
A sudden surge in gold supply drives its purchasing power down

explanation: Mali's emperor distributed so much gold in Egypt that gold's local value fell and prices of everyday goods jumped for years.

trap_notes.a: Value fell from oversupply in an active market, not from a trade ban.
trap_notes.b: Spending, not taxing, flooded Cairo's economy with extra gold.
trap_notes.c: An abundance of gold, not a shortage, caused prices to rise.
trap_notes.default: Even commodity money like gold loses purchasing power when supply surges.

prompt: How did the U.S. Constitution's Interstate Commerce Clause fix a major flaw of the Articles of Confederation?

options.text: It barred states from taxing each other's goods, creating a common market
It required every state to print its own separate paper currency
It gave state governors sole power over foreign trade treaties
It abolished all federal customs duties at Atlantic seaports

explanation: Giving Congress power over interstate trade ended state-versus-state tariff wars and fostered a unified national market.

trap_notes.b: The Constitution prohibited states from coining money or issuing bills of credit.
trap_notes.c: Foreign commerce power was placed in Congress, not state governors.
trap_notes.d: Congress gained power to levy uniform federal tariffs at national ports.
trap_notes.default: The Commerce Clause stopped state trade wars and built a single U.S. market.

prompt: What economic incentive explains the U.S. Constitution's Patent and Copyright Clause in Article I, Section 8?

options.text: Forcing inventors to share trade secrets with rivals free of charge
Granting temporary exclusive rights so creators can recoup R&D costs
Creating permanent government monopolies over all retail stores
Eliminating private property rights in books and software

explanation: Limited-time patents and copyrights reward innovation by preventing immediate copying, while later entering the public domain.

trap_notes.a: Patents protect inventors from immediate copying rather than forcing free sharing.
trap_notes.c: Patents are temporary and cover specific inventions, not permanent retail monopolies.
trap_notes.d: Copyrights establish intellectual property rights rather than removing them.
trap_notes.default: Temporary intellectual property rights incentivize costly research and creation.

prompt: How does the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause protect market incentives when government uses eminent domain?

options.text: It bars governments from ever building public highways
It lets local mayors seize factories without paying owners
It requires just compensation for private land taken for public use
It exempts commercial real estate from all state property taxes

explanation: Requiring fair market payment disciplines government land seizures and preserves investor confidence in property rights.

trap_notes.a: Government can build highways if it pays just compensation for private land.
trap_notes.b: Uncompensated seizure violates the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause.
trap_notes.d: The Takings Clause governs condemnation, not routine property taxation.
trap_notes.default: Just compensation protects property owners when land is taken for public use.

prompt: How did the Sixteenth Amendment (1913) change federal revenue and fiscal policy?

options.text: It replaced all federal taxes with a national sales tax
It required Congress to balance the federal budget every month
It transferred income-tax collection solely to state governors
It authorized a progressive federal tax on individual incomes

explanation: The 16th Amendment allowed Congress to tax incomes directly without apportioning by state population, shifting away from tariffs.

trap_notes.a: The United States has never enacted a national retail sales tax.
trap_notes.b: The 16th Amendment created revenue authority, not a balanced-budget rule.
trap_notes.c: It empowered Congress, not state governors, to levy federal income taxes.
trap_notes.default: The 16th Amendment enabled the modern federal income tax.

prompt: What two statutory goals form the Federal Reserve's dual mandate assigned by Congress?

options.text: Maximum employment and stable prices
Zero national debt and fixed exchange rates
Rising stock prices and balanced trade
Low corporate taxes and high tariffs

explanation: Congress amended the Federal Reserve Act in 1977 to direct monetary policy toward maximum employment and price stability.

trap_notes.b: Fiscal deficits and floating exchange rates are outside the Fed's dual mandate.
trap_notes.c: The Fed watches financial stability, not specific stock-index or trade-balance targets.
trap_notes.d: Tax rates and tariffs are set by Congress, not the Federal Reserve.
trap_notes.default: The Fed's statutory dual mandate is maximum employment and price stability.

prompt: Why do democracies give central banks operational independence from short-term election politics?

options.text: So central banks can write federal tax laws without Congress
So policymakers can fight inflation without pre-election rate cuts
So voters cannot see annual unemployment or CPI statistics
So private banks can set federal minimum wage rates

explanation: Independent central banks resist political pressure to print money or cut rates before elections, anchoring low inflation expectations.

trap_notes.a: Congress retains all taxing and spending authority under the Constitution.
trap_notes.c: Central banks publish data openly; independence insulates rate decisions.
trap_notes.d: Minimum wage laws are set by legislatures, not private banks.
trap_notes.default: Central bank independence prevents politically timed inflation cycles.

prompt: How do city and state governments typically finance long-lived public schools, bridges, and water systems?

options.text: By printing their own state paper currency
By borrowing directly from the World Trade Organization
By issuing tax-exempt municipal bonds to investors
By levying protective tariffs on neighboring states

explanation: Municipal bonds let local governments spread infrastructure costs over decades while offering investors tax-advantaged interest.

trap_notes.a: The U.S. Constitution prohibits states from issuing their own currency.
trap_notes.b: The WTO sets trade rules; it does not lend money to U.S. cities.
trap_notes.d: States cannot tax interstate imports under the Commerce Clause.
trap_notes.default: Municipal bonds fund long-term state and local capital projects.

prompt: What public-choice problem occurs when a government regulatory agency ends up serving the industry it oversees?

options.text: Creative destruction
Comparative advantage
Monetary neutrality
Regulatory capture

explanation: Regulatory capture happens when concentrated industry lobbying steers rules toward incumbent profits instead of public safety.

trap_notes.a: Creative destruction describes new innovations displacing older firms.
trap_notes.b: Comparative advantage explains specialization in international trade.
trap_notes.c: Monetary neutrality means money supply changes affect prices, not real output, long term.
trap_notes.default: Regulatory capture occurs when agencies favor regulated firms over the public.

prompt: In fiscal federalism, why does Congress attach conditions to categorical grants sent to state governments?

options.text: To ensure states spend federal funds on specific national priorities
To prevent states from collecting any local sales or property taxes
To let state legislatures set national monetary policy rates
To replace state governors with federal treasury officials

explanation: Categorical grants fund defined areas like highways or Medicaid and require states to follow federal standards.

trap_notes.b: States retain independent authority to levy state sales, income, and property taxes.
trap_notes.c: Monetary policy belongs solely to the Federal Reserve, not state legislatures.
trap_notes.d: Grants use financial incentives rather than replacing elected state leaders.
trap_notes.default: Categorical grants steer state spending toward targeted federal goals.

prompt: How does a cap-and-trade emissions system differ from a flat carbon tax in curbing pollution?

options.text: Cap-and-trade bans all electricity generation from fossil fuels
Cap-and-trade fixes total emissions while letting permit prices float
Cap-and-trade pays factories a bonus for each ton of carbon
Cap-and-trade sets a fixed tax rate with no limit on total tons

explanation: Cap-and-trade caps overall pollution and lets firms trade permits; a carbon tax fixes the price per ton instead.

trap_notes.a: Firms can still emit carbon if they buy or hold enough permits under the cap.
trap_notes.c: Firms pay for permits or invest in cleaner tech; they are not paid to pollute.
trap_notes.d: Fixing the price per ton without a quantity cap describes a carbon tax.
trap_notes.default: Cap-and-trade sets a quantity ceiling, whereas a carbon tax sets a price.

prompt: What labor-market floor did the 1938 Fair Labor Standards Act establish nationwide?

options.text: Lifetime guaranteed employment in federal agencies
Mandatory profit-sharing for every agricultural worker
A federal minimum wage, overtime pay, and child-labor limits
Annual wage freezes across all unionized manufacturing

explanation: The Fair Labor Standards Act created the federal minimum wage, time-and-a-half overtime, and restrictions on child labor.

trap_notes.a: The act regulated private-sector pay and hours rather than guaranteeing federal jobs.
trap_notes.b: The law did not mandate profit-sharing and initially exempted many farmworkers.
trap_notes.d: It set a wage floor rather than freezing wages.
trap_notes.default: The 1938 FLSA established the federal minimum wage and overtime rules.

prompt: How did predictable seasonal monsoon winds shape Indian Ocean trade before steamships?

options.text: Merchants avoided sailing between East Africa and India altogether
High winds forced traders to carry spices overland across Siberia
Year-round storms prevented any port cities from developing
Reversing winds timed round-trip voyages and grew port entrepots

explanation: Southwest summer monsoons blew ships toward India, and northeast winter winds carried them back to Arabia and East Africa.

trap_notes.a: Monsoon winds made Indian Ocean crossings faster and safer than open-Atlantic routes.
trap_notes.b: Indian Ocean spice trade moved overwhelmingly by sea, not across Siberia.
trap_notes.c: Waiting between wind shifts turned ports like Calicut and Kilwa into thriving hubs.
trap_notes.default: Predictable reversing monsoons structured round-trip Indian Ocean shipping.

prompt: Why do landlocked developing countries often face slower trade growth than coastal nations?

options.text: Overland transit and border delays raise import and export costs
International law forbids landlocked states from joining the WTO
Coastal countries refuse to buy any agricultural goods
Landlocked economies cannot use paper currency or banks

explanation: Relying on neighbors' highways, rails, and seaports adds transit fees and customs delays that raise trade costs.

trap_notes.b: Many landlocked nations, such as Bolivia and Uganda, are WTO members.
trap_notes.c: Coastal nations import farm and mineral goods from inland neighbors.
trap_notes.d: Landlocked countries maintain normal currencies and banking systems.
trap_notes.default: Lack of direct sea access raises overland freight and border transit costs.

prompt: Why do competing technology or finance firms often cluster in the same city despite high office rents?

options.text: Federal zoning laws forbid startups from opening elsewhere
Clustering yields deep talent pools and fast knowledge spillovers
High rents automatically lower corporate income tax rates
Rival firms share identical bank accounts to cut costs

explanation: Agglomeration economies give clustered firms easier access to specialized workers, suppliers, and informal ideas.

trap_notes.a: Firms cluster voluntarily for productivity gains, not due to federal bans.
trap_notes.c: High rents are a cost of clustering, offset by productivity advantages.
trap_notes.d: Competing firms remain separate businesses even when located nearby.
trap_notes.default: Agglomeration economies reward firms for locating near talent and suppliers.

prompt: What economic distortion does the term 'Dutch Disease' describe in resource-rich countries?

options.text: Crop blights that wipe out agricultural exports
Central bank deflation caused by running out of oil
Resource booms driving up currency value and hurting factories
Falling tax revenues when ports handle too much cargo

explanation: A surge in oil or gas exports appreciates the currency, making the country's non-resource exports less competitive abroad.

trap_notes.a: Dutch Disease is a macroeconomic currency effect, not a plant disease.
trap_notes.b: It stems from booming resource revenues, not resource exhaustion.
trap_notes.d: Higher export volumes usually raise port activity rather than cutting port fees.
trap_notes.default: Resource booms appreciate the currency and squeeze manufacturing exports.

prompt: Why did Panama build wider Neopanamax canal locks that opened in 2016?

options.text: To drain Gatun Lake and turn the route into a highway
To block U.S. liquefied natural gas tankers from Asia
To replace the Suez Canal for Europe-to-India shipping
To fit larger container ships and capture economies of scale

explanation: Wider locks let modern megaships carry nearly triple the cargo per transit, lowering per-container shipping costs.

trap_notes.a: Gatun Lake remains essential to operating the canal's lock system.
trap_notes.b: Expanded locks actually opened a major route for U.S. LNG exports to Asia.
trap_notes.c: Europe-to-India trade still relies on the Suez Canal rather than Panama.
trap_notes.default: Larger locks allow megaships to lower per-unit ocean freight costs.

prompt: Why do electronics and wind-turbine makers worry about geographic concentration in rare-earth processing?

options.text: Export limits in one dominant supplier can disrupt global supply
Rare-earth metals are only used to print paper banknotes
Rare earths cannot be transported aboard cargo ships
Every country already refines equal amounts of rare earths

explanation: Because China refines most global rare-earth elements, supply-chain bottlenecks or export curbs can stall high-tech output.

trap_notes.b: Rare earths are vital for magnets, batteries, motors, and optics, not banknotes.
trap_notes.c: Refined rare-earth oxides and magnets are routinely shipped worldwide.
trap_notes.d: Processing capacity is heavily concentrated rather than evenly distributed.
trap_notes.default: Geographic concentration in critical minerals creates supply-chain risk.

prompt: What economic tradeoff caused the shrinking of Central Asia's Aral Sea since the 1960s?

options.text: Building hydroelectric dams to flood coastal cotton fields
Diverting feeder rivers for irrigated cotton at fishery expense
Rising ocean tides draining an inland freshwater lake
Overfishing sturgeon without any agricultural irrigation

explanation: Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya for desert cotton, collapsing the Aral Sea and its fishing economy.

trap_notes.a: River water was diverted away into irrigation canals rather than flooding the basin.
trap_notes.c: The Aral Sea is an endorheic inland lake disconnected from ocean tides.
trap_notes.d: Massive irrigation diversion, not fishing alone, shrank the sea.
trap_notes.default: Diverting river water for cotton destroyed the Aral Sea's fishery and ecology.

prompt: Why did major trade cities grow at 'break-of-bulk' points such as river fall lines and deepwater ports?

options.text: Governments banned warehouses anywhere along coastlines
Traders had to pay zero wages at river waterfalls
Cargo shifted transport modes there, spawning storage and trade
All inland rivers freeze solid throughout the summer

explanation: Unloading goods from ships to barges, wagons, or rail created jobs in warehousing, finance, and local processing.

trap_notes.a: Ports and fall-line cities actually concentrated warehouses and docks.
trap_notes.b: Workers earned normal wages handling and processing cargo.
trap_notes.d: Break-of-bulk points reflect terrain and ship-size limits, not summer ice.
trap_notes.default: Transferring cargo between transport modes builds commercial cities.

prompt: What macroeconomic challenge does rapid population aging pose to countries like Japan?

options.text: Too many teenagers entering entry-level factory jobs
Surging birthrates forcing cuts in pension spending
Falling retiree numbers lowering healthcare demand
A shrinking workforce supporting a rising share of retirees

explanation: Fewer working-age adults slow potential GDP growth while increasing pension and healthcare burdens per worker.

trap_notes.a: Aging societies face labor shortages rather than an oversupply of young workers.
trap_notes.b: Low birthrates, not surging birthrates, drive demographic aging.
trap_notes.c: Older populations increase demand for healthcare and pensions.
trap_notes.default: Population aging shrinks the labor force relative to retirees.

prompt: How do migrant worker remittances affect developing economies such as the Philippines or Mexico?

options.text: They bring foreign currency that lifts household spending and reserves
They count as domestic factory output inside U.S. GDP
They force home-country central banks to print less currency
They eliminate the need for commercial banks in rural towns

explanation: Money sent home by overseas workers boosts family consumption, education spending, and national foreign-exchange inflows.

trap_notes.b: Transfers across borders are personal income flows, not U.S. factory output.
trap_notes.c: Remittances add foreign currency inflows rather than shrinking domestic money.
trap_notes.d: Banks and money-transfer firms are the channels used to deliver remittances.
trap_notes.default: Remittances provide vital foreign-exchange and household income inflows.

prompt: Why do economists call an automaker's demand for assembly-line workers a 'derived demand'?

options.text: Labor demand depends on consumer demand for finished cars
Workers set their own hourly wages without market input
Auto plants hire workers only during economic recessions
Government labor boards assign workers to factories

explanation: Firms hire inputs like labor because consumers want the final product; when car sales rise, labor demand rises too.

trap_notes.b: Wages reflect supply and demand for labor, not unilateral worker pricing.
trap_notes.c: Recessions reduce car demand and typically lower hiring.
trap_notes.d: In market economies, firms decide hiring based on expected product sales.
trap_notes.default: Input demand is derived from demand for the final good it helps produce.

prompt: If the price of peanut butter jumps sharply and consumers buy less jelly, how are peanut butter and jelly related?

options.text: They are substitute goods
They are complementary goods
They are inferior goods
They are pure public goods

explanation: Complementary goods are used together; a higher price for one reduces demand for the other (negative cross-price elasticity).

trap_notes.a: If they were substitutes, a higher peanut butter price would raise jelly demand.
trap_notes.c: Inferior goods depend on consumer income changes, not another good's price.
trap_notes.d: Both peanut butter and jelly are rivalrous, excludable private goods.
trap_notes.default: When a price hike in one good cuts demand for another, they are complements.

prompt: In George Akerlof's used-car 'lemons' problem, what market failure arises from asymmetric information?

options.text: Sellers charge lower prices than buyers offer
High-quality cars flood the market at bargain rates
Buyers offer low prices, driving good cars out of the market
Automakers stop building new vehicles altogether

explanation: When buyers cannot tell good cars from defects, they discount offers, causing owners of good cars to withdraw (adverse selection).

trap_notes.a: Buyers discount offers because they fear hidden defects, not because sellers underprice.
trap_notes.b: Good-car owners exit the market rather than selling at low average prices.
trap_notes.d: The lemons problem affects used markets with hidden quality, not new-car production.
trap_notes.default: Hidden quality causes adverse selection that pushes high-quality goods out.

prompt: Which situation best illustrates 'moral hazard' in insurance or banking?

options.text: A driver buys a safer car after reading crash ratings
A homeowner installs smoke detectors to cut premiums
A saver compares interest rates across three banks
An insured bank takes riskier bets expecting a bailout

explanation: Moral hazard occurs after a contract is signed when protection from losses encourages someone to take greater risks.

trap_notes.a: Choosing a safer vehicle reduces risk rather than increasing it.
trap_notes.b: Installing smoke detectors lowers fire risk.
trap_notes.c: Shopping for interest rates is normal market comparison, not risk-taking.
trap_notes.default: Moral hazard happens when being shielded from loss encourages riskier behavior.

prompt: A student buys a nonrefundable $15 ticket, dislikes the movie, yet stays only because they already paid. What error is this?

options.text: Sunk cost fallacy
Price discrimination
Liquidity trap
Purchasing power parity

explanation: A sunk cost cannot be recovered; rational choices weigh only future marginal benefits and costs, not past unrecoverable spending.

trap_notes.b: Price discrimination is charging different buyers different prices for the same good.
trap_notes.c: A liquidity trap occurs when near-zero interest rates fail to spur borrowing.
trap_notes.d: Purchasing power parity compares currency values across countries.
trap_notes.default: The sunk cost fallacy lets unrecoverable past expenses distort future choices.

prompt: When does a manufacturing firm experience economies of scale in the long run?

options.text: When its total fixed costs fall to zero after one week
When its average total cost per unit falls as output grows
When its product price rises faster than worker wages
When government regulators cap its annual factory output

explanation: Economies of scale occur when expanding plant size and specialization lowers the long-run average cost of each unit produced.

trap_notes.a: Fixed costs remain positive; they spread across more units per period.
trap_notes.c: Economies of scale measure falling unit production costs, not rising prices.
trap_notes.d: Output caps restrict scale rather than creating cost efficiencies.
trap_notes.default: Economies of scale mean lower average cost per unit at higher output.

prompt: Why are international producer cartels such as OPEC often unstable over time?

options.text: Consumers stop using energy whenever prices rise slightly
Cartel rules force every member to cut output to zero
Each member can profit by secretly producing above its quota
Central banks outlaw oil trading across national borders

explanation: When a cartel restricts supply to lift prices, individual members face a prisoner's dilemma incentive to cheat and sell extra barrels.

trap_notes.a: Oil demand is relatively price inelastic in the short run.
trap_notes.b: Cartels set production quotas, not zero output.
trap_notes.d: Oil is actively traded globally across currencies and borders.
trap_notes.default: High cartel prices tempt individual members to cheat on output quotas.

prompt: What does 'crowding out' mean when a government runs large budget deficits during full employment?

options.text: Lower income taxes force households to work fewer hours
Commercial banks close local branches due to low deposits
Rising exports push domestic consumer goods off store shelves
Heavy public borrowing lifts interest rates and curbs private investment

explanation: When government competes for limited loanable funds, higher real interest rates can reduce private business capital spending.

trap_notes.a: Lower income taxes generally raise, not lower, the incentive to work.
trap_notes.b: Crowding out is an interest-rate effect in credit markets, not branch closures.
trap_notes.c: Higher interest rates tend to appreciate currency and reduce net exports.
trap_notes.default: Government deficit borrowing can push up rates and crowd out private investment.

prompt: In the equation of exchange (M x V = P x Q), what does the 'velocity of money' (V) measure?

options.text: How many times an average dollar is spent on final goods yearly
How fast armored trucks deliver coins to retail banks
The percentage interest rate charged on 30-year mortgages
The annual trade deficit divided by total tariff revenue

explanation: Velocity measures how rapidly money circulates through the economy to buy final goods and services in a given period.

trap_notes.b: Velocity tracks economic turnover of spending, not physical cash transport.
trap_notes.c: Mortgage rates reflect credit pricing, not spending turnover.
trap_notes.d: Trade deficits and tariffs are international trade figures, not money velocity.
trap_notes.default: Velocity is the average number of times a dollar is spent in a year.

prompt: Why do economists use Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) instead of market exchange rates to compare living standards?

options.text: Market exchange rates exclude all stock market investments
PPP adjusts for differences in local prices of everyday goods
PPP ignores services such as housing and local haircuts
Market exchange rates remain fixed by the United Nations

explanation: Because haircuts, rent, and local food often cost less in lower-income countries, PPP compares what incomes actually buy.

trap_notes.a: GDP comparisons measure output and consumption, not stock holdings.
trap_notes.c: PPP specifically accounts for non-traded local services like housing and haircuts.
trap_notes.d: Major market exchange rates float daily on foreign-exchange markets.
trap_notes.default: PPP adjusts currency comparisons for local cost-of-living differences.

prompt: How does Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) differ from foreign portfolio investment?

options.text: FDI only buys short-term government treasury bills
FDI requires zero physical assets in the host country
FDI involves lasting ownership and control of foreign operations
FDI is restricted strictly to domestic municipal bonds

explanation: Building a factory or acquiring a controlling stake abroad is FDI, whereas buying small stock or bond stakes is portfolio investment.

trap_notes.a: Buying short-term treasury bills is liquid portfolio investment, not FDI.
trap_notes.b: FDI typically builds or acquires physical plants, equipment, or subsidiaries.
trap_notes.d: FDI crosses national borders rather than staying inside domestic municipal bonds.
trap_notes.default: FDI creates lasting operational control in a foreign business or facility.

prompt: In a nation's balance of payments, which transaction is recorded in the current account?

options.text: A foreign bank purchasing U.S. Treasury bonds
A domestic firm building an auto plant overseas
A central bank buying gold bars from another central bank
A domestic airline selling tickets to foreign tourists

explanation: The current account tracks exports and imports of goods and services (including tourism), plus primary income and transfers.

trap_notes.a: Cross-border bond purchases belong in the financial account.
trap_notes.b: Building a foreign factory is direct investment in the financial account.
trap_notes.c: Official reserve transactions appear in the financial account.
trap_notes.default: Exports and imports of goods and services belong in the current account.

prompt: Why does paying only the minimum monthly payment on a high-APR credit card cost a borrower far more over time?

options.text: Unpaid principal keeps compounding high interest every billing cycle
Credit card issuers double the purchase price after thirty days
Minimum payments lower the card's APR to zero percent
Federal law forbids borrowers from paying off balances early

explanation: Small minimum payments mostly cover interest, leaving principal unpaid and compounding heavy debt costs.

trap_notes.b: The sticker price stays fixed; compounding interest on the unpaid balance adds cost.
trap_notes.c: Carrying a balance keeps the regular APR active rather than dropping it to zero.
trap_notes.d: Borrowers can pay off credit card balances in full anytime without penalty.
trap_notes.default: Small minimum payments leave principal unpaid, compounding high interest.

prompt: How does a Roth IRA differ from a Traditional IRA for retirement savers?

options.text: Roth IRAs are funded with pre-tax income and taxed at withdrawal
Roth IRAs are funded with after-tax income for tax-free withdrawals
Roth IRAs guarantee a fixed 10 percent return from the Treasury
Roth IRAs allow zero stock or index-fund investments

explanation: Roth IRA contributions are taxed upfront, allowing qualified investment growth and retirement withdrawals to be tax-free.

trap_notes.a: Pre-tax contributions and taxed withdrawals describe a Traditional IRA.
trap_notes.c: IRA returns depend on chosen market investments, not a Treasury guarantee.
trap_notes.d: Roth IRAs commonly hold stocks, bonds, and mutual or index funds.
trap_notes.default: Roth IRAs tax contributions today so qualified withdrawals are tax-free.

prompt: Why do many long-term investors prefer broad stock index funds over actively managed mutual funds?

options.text: Index funds eliminate all risk of stock market downturns
Index funds are insured against loss by the FDIC
Index funds charge lower fees and track broad market returns
Index funds pay no capital gains taxes when sold at a profit

explanation: Passive index funds avoid costly stock-picking research, keeping expense ratios low while diversifying across the entire index.

trap_notes.a: Index funds still rise and fall with the overall stock market.
trap_notes.b: FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, not stock market index funds.
trap_notes.d: Profits from selling index funds in taxable accounts remain subject to capital gains tax.
trap_notes.default: Low expense ratios and broad diversification make index funds popular.
